name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Increasing boiling points of hydrogen isotopes

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following isotopic forms of dihydrogen in increasing order of their boiling points:

(I) Tritium (\(\mathrm{T}_2\))
(II) Protium (\(\mathrm{H}_2\))
(III) Deuterium (\(\mathrm{D}_2\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although the isotopes of hydrogen have identical electronic configurations and nearly identical chemical properties, their physical properties—such as melting point, boiling point, and density—differ significantly due to large relative differences in their atomic and molecular masses.

Step 2: Evaluation of Boiling Points
From the physical property data of hydrogen isotopes:
- Protium (\(\mathrm{H}_2\), relative atomic mass \(1.008\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) has a boiling point of \(20.39\text{ K}\).
- Deuterium (\(\mathrm{D}_2\), relative atomic mass \(2.014\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) has a boiling point of \(23.67\text{ K}\).
- Tritium (\(\mathrm{T}_2\), relative atomic mass \(3.016\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) has a boiling point of \(25.0\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
As isotopic mass increases, intermolecular van der Waals forces and boiling points increase. Therefore, the increasing order of boiling points is Protium (\(\mathrm{H}_2\)) < Deuterium (\(\mathrm{D}_2\)) < Tritium (\(\mathrm{T}_2\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Steps in dihydrogen production from coal

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps involved in the commercial production of pure dihydrogen from coal in the correct sequential order:

(I) Scrubbing the gas mixture with sodium arsenite solution to remove \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)
(II) Coal gasification: reacting \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s})\) with steam at \(1270\text{ K}\) to produce syngas (\(\mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{H}_2\))
(III) Water-gas shift reaction: reacting \(\mathrm{CO}\) of syngas with steam at \(673\text{ K}\) over iron chromate catalyst to form \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Producing pure dihydrogen from solid carbon (coal) requires first converting it into synthesis gas, then increasing the \(\mathrm{H}_2\) yield via the water-gas shift reaction, and finally removing the \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) byproduct.

Step 2: Sequential Analysis of Stages
1. First, coal gasification converts coke and steam at \(1270\text{ K}\) into syngas: \[\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow{1270\text{ K}} \mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\]
2. Next, the carbon monoxide in the syngas mixture is reacted with steam at \(673\text{ K}\) in the presence of an iron chromate catalyst (water-gas shift reaction) to generate additional dihydrogen: \[\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow[\text{catalyst}]{673\text{ K}} \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\]
3. Finally, the carbon dioxide formed is removed by scrubbing the gas mixture with sodium arsenite solution, leaving pure dihydrogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is coal gasification, followed by the water-gas shift reaction, and then scrubbing with sodium arsenite solution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Demineralisation of water using synthetic resins

questiontext.text:
Arrange the stages in the preparation of pure demineralised water using synthetic ion-exchange resins in the correct operational order:

(I) Neutralisation of liberated \(\mathrm{H}^+\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions to form \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\)
(II) Passing hard water through a cation-exchange resin in the \(\mathrm{H}^+\) form, releasing \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions
(III) Passing the acidic water through an anion-exchange resin in the \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) form, releasing \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions
(IV) Regenerating the exhausted cation and anion resin beds with dilute acid and alkali solutions respectively

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Demineralised (de-ionised) water free from all soluble mineral salts is obtained by sequentially removing all cations and all anions using synthetic ion-exchange resins.

Step 2: Sequential Analysis of Stages
1. Hard water is first passed through a cation-exchange resin in the \(\mathrm{H}^+\) form (\(\mathrm{RH}\)), where \(\mathrm{H}^+\) exchanges for \(\mathrm{Na}^+\), \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\), and other cations, making the effluent acidic.
2. This acidic water is then passed through an anion-exchange resin in the \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) form (\(\mathrm{RNH}_3^+\cdot\mathrm{OH}^-\)), where \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) exchanges for anions such as \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\), \(\mathrm{HCO}_3^-\), and \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\).
3. The \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions thus liberated neutralise the \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions set free in the cation-exchange step to form pure water (\(\mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{OH}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)).
4. Once the resin beds are exhausted, they are regenerated by treating the cation exchanger with dilute acid and the anion exchanger with dilute alkali.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is cation exchange, followed by anion exchange, then neutralisation to form water, and finally regeneration of the exhausted resin beds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Industrial synthesis and concentration of H2O2

questiontext.text:
Arrange the steps in the industrial manufacture and purification of pure hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) in the correct chronological sequence:

(I) Concentration to \(\sim 30\%\) (by mass) by distillation under reduced pressure
(II) Extraction of the \(1\%\) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) formed with water
(III) Auto-oxidation of 2-ethylanthraquinol with \(\mathrm{O}_2\) (air)
(IV) Further concentration to \(\sim 85\%\) by careful distillation under low pressure, followed by freezing out the remaining water

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Industrially, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is produced via the cyclic auto-oxidation of 2-alkylanthraquinols and must be concentrated gently under reduced pressure because \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) decomposes on heating at atmospheric pressure.

Step 2: Sequential Analysis of Stages
1. First, 2-ethylanthraquinol undergoes auto-oxidation with atmospheric \(\mathrm{O}_2\) to yield \(1\%\) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) (alongside 2-ethylanthraquinone, which is reduced back with \(\mathrm{H}_2/\mathrm{Pd}\)).
2. Next, the \(1\%\) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is extracted from the organic phase using water.
3. The aqueous solution is concentrated to \(\sim 30\%\) (by mass) by distillation under reduced pressure.
4. Finally, it is further concentrated to \(\sim 85\%\) by careful distillation under low pressure, and the remaining water is frozen out to obtain pure \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct order is auto-oxidation, water extraction, reduced-pressure distillation to \(\sim 30\%\), and low-pressure distillation to \(\sim 85\%\) followed by freezing out water.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Increasing ionic character of alkali metal hydrides

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following saline hydrides in increasing order of their ionic character:

\(\mathrm{LiH}\), \(\mathrm{NaH}\), \(\mathrm{CsH}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionic (saline) hydrides are formed by \(s\)-block elements. However, lighter metal hydrides such as \(\mathrm{LiH}\) possess significant covalent character due to the small size and high polarising power of the \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) cation (Fajans' rules), as well as lower electropositivity compared to heavier alkali metals.

Step 2: Evaluation Down the Group
Moving down Group 1 from \(\mathrm{Li}\) to \(\mathrm{Na}\) to \(\mathrm{Cs}\), atomic/ionic size increases, polarising power of the cation decreases, and electropositive character increases. Consequently, the ionic character of the metal–hydrogen bond increases steadily from \(\mathrm{LiH}\) to \(\mathrm{NaH}\) to \(\mathrm{CsH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the increasing order of ionic character is \(\mathrm{LiH} < \mathrm{NaH} < \mathrm{CsH}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Increasing bond dissociation enthalpy of diatomic molecules

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following covalent single bonds in increasing order of bond dissociation enthalpy:

\(\mathrm{F-F}\), \(\mathrm{H-H}\), \(\mathrm{D-D}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The \(\mathrm{H-H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy is the highest for a single bond between two atoms of any element, and isotopic substitution by the heavier deuterium atom further increases the bond dissociation enthalpy due to lower zero-point vibrational energy.

Step 2: Quantitative Comparison
- For \(\mathrm{F-F}\), interelectronic repulsion between the non-bonding lone pairs on the small fluorine atoms weakens the single bond, giving a much lower bond dissociation enthalpy (\(\sim 158\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).
- For \(\mathrm{H-H}\) at \(298.2\text{ K}\), the bond dissociation enthalpy is \(435.88\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
- For \(\mathrm{D-D}\) at \(298.2\text{ K}\), the bond dissociation enthalpy is \(443.35\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the increasing order of bond dissociation enthalpy is \(\mathrm{F-F} < \mathrm{H-H} < \mathrm{D-D}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_SEQUENCING_Q07 - Decreasing order of world water supply sources

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following sources of the estimated world water supply in decreasing order of their percentage of total water:

(I) Ground water
(II) Oceans
(III) Polar ice and glaciers
(IV) Lakes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The distribution of water over the earth's surface is highly uneven, with the vast majority stored in oceans and most freshwater locked in polar ice and glaciers.

Step 2: Quantitative Comparison
According to the estimated world water supply:
- Oceans account for \(97.33\%\) of total water.
- Polar ice and glaciers account for \(2.04\%\).
- Ground water accounts for \(0.61\%\).
- Lakes account for \(0.009\%\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Comparing these percentages gives the decreasing order: Oceans (\(97.33\%\)) > Polar ice and glaciers (\(2.04\%\)) > Ground water (\(0.61\%\)) > Lakes (\(0.009\%\)).
